content:
Here is a note offered by a side agent:

> Heads up · The new linter setup checks fewer things than Biome did, because the main agent turned on only oxlint's "correctness" rules and switched a few rules off.
>
> **The new oxlint setup checks less than Biome did**
> * **Before:** Biome ran its recommended rule set. That set included "suspicious" checks, such as a warning when `${...}` sits in a normal string where a template string was probably meant.
> * **Now:** `.oxlintrc.json` turns on only oxlint's **correctness** group of rules. It also switches off four rules: control characters in regex, needless spread, `expect` inside conditions, and the argument limit on `expect` (now allows 2).
> * The old `biome-ignore` comments are now plain comments, because the rule they silenced is not on any more.
> * The main agent did this because stricter groups flagged about 150 issues, many of them false alarms.
> * **If you want Biome-level coverage back, consider turning on the "suspicious" group as warnings** and working through what it finds.

questions.question: Your ~/.claude/settings.json still runs the Python hooks (rm_rf_guard, dangerous_commands, secrets_guard, config_guard, file_protection, bash_risk_judge) on every tool call. With the mod installed too, every call gets judged twice. How should I install and test the mod?

options.label: Clean test session (Recommended)
options.description: Don't install anything. I give you a command for a second terminal: `claude --setting-sources project,local --plugin-dir ~/Develop/claude-decisions-mod`. It loads only the mod, without your user hooks, and reloads it when you save a file.

options.label: Install now, keep Python
options.description: Add this folder as a local marketplace, install decisions-guard, then you run /reload-plugins here. This session judges every call twice until you remove the Python hooks.

options.label: Install, you drop Python
options.description: I install from the local folder. You remove the Python PreToolUse hooks from settings.json yourself (config-guard stops me from editing it), then run /reload-plugins.

questions.question: `typesafe-ai/jev` still serves the older weights (outputs differ from 1.14.0). In my probe (111 cases × 2 runs), 1.14.0 caught more (persistence 12/16 vs 9/16, covers_tracks 10/10 vs 8/10) and was a bit faster (p95 0.63s vs 0.73s). But it prompted on `terraform plan` twice (credential_store 0.71/0.72, just over the 0.7 threshold), and it has no DigitalOcean fallback. Which default should the mod use?

options.label: Keep typesafe-ai/jev (Recommended)
options.description: No false prompts on benign commands, plus a provider fallback. The alias should move to 1.14 when TypeSafe promotes it.

options.label: Pin jev-1.14.0
options.description: Higher recall, but it has no fallback, occasional prompts on `terraform plan`, and you have to bump the pin by hand.

content.text:
You wanted to clarify my two questions, so I've stopped there. Nothing is installed, your settings are unchanged, and nothing is committed. Here is where things stand.

## Linter and formatter: Biome replaced by oxlint and oxfmt
- **Removed:** `biome.json` and `@biomejs/biome`.
- **Formatter:** `.oxfmtrc.json` came from `oxfmt --migrate=biome`, so it keeps 4-space indent, 110 columns and double quotes. I excluded `*.md`, because Biome never formatted Markdown and oxfmt would rewrite every table. Running it reformatted 3 files slightly (`engine-host.ts`, `writes.ts`, `package.json`).
- **Scripts:** `lint` now runs `oxlint --deny-warnings && oxfmt --check`. `format` runs `oxfmt`. There is a new `lint:fix`.
- **Two small fixes the linter asked for:** `new Array(n)` in `scripts/script-support.ts` and a redundant length check in `scripts/judge-probe.ts`.
- **Old suppression comments:** The `biome-ignore` comments are now plain comments. They kept their explanation, such as "a shell spelling of HOME, not a template".
- **README:** updated the dev commands. I also fixed the credential order it listed. The code reads the `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` and `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` environment variables before the `jevApiKey` option, not after.

**About the side note:** it's right that oxlint now checks less than Biome did. `.oxlintrc.json` turns on only the correctness rules, and switches off four rules for these reasons:
- **Control characters in regex:** Biome had this rule off too.
- **Needless spread:** a false alarm. At `src/shell/unwrap.ts:188` the spread splits a string into characters, and the other hits copy a Map's keys on purpose before deleting from it.
- **`expect` inside conditions:** the table-driven tests rely on it.
- **`expect` argument limit:** raised to 2, because vitest accepts `expect(value, message)`.

Adding the suspicious rules as warnings turns up about 150 hits. 77 of them flag `${...}` in plain strings, mostly tests that spell shell syntax on purpose; Biome needed only 13 suppressions for the same thing. The rest are 26 shadowed variables, 21 `.sort()` calls and 14 functions that could move out of their parent. Since `lint` fails on any warning, turning that group on means working through all of it first. I'd do that as a separate change.

## Checks
All pass: oxlint, oxfmt, 7,648 vitest tests, `tsc`, `claude plugin validate` and `claude plugin test` (7/7).
- **Tests:** two `config-guard` tests were already failing before my changes, only on macOS. The temp folder `/var/...` is a link to `/private/var/...`, which added an extra path form. I fixed the test setup to resolve the real temp path; the guard code was correct.
- **Typecheck:** it needs `.claude-plugin/types`, a git-ignored folder that Claude Code writes when it loads the mod. This checkout didn't have it yet, so I copied this build's types in.

## Jev with ai 0.7
The new version works with the existing client unchanged. The gateway lists `typesafe-ai/jev`, `jev-1.13.0` and `jev-1.14.0`. The fnox lookup also works with no key in the environment: I ran the judge from `/`, it found the key, and there were 0 errors.

I ran the probe script on 111 cases, twice each:

| | `typesafe-ai/jev` (alias) | `jev-1.14.0` |
|---|---|---|
| Persistence caught | 9/16 | 12/16 |
| Covering tracks caught | 8/10 | 10/10 |
| False prompts on harmless commands | 0/56 | 2/56 (`terraform plan`, 0.71 and 0.72 against the 0.7 threshold) |
| p95 latency | 0.73s | 0.63s |
| Backup provider | DigitalOcean | none |

The alias's answers differ from 1.14.0's, so it most likely still serves the older 1.13 weights. I left the default as the alias.

## Do you need a separate session?
Not necessarily. You could add this folder as a local marketplace, install the mod, and run `/reload-plugins` here. But `~/.claude/settings.json` still runs all six Python hooks, so with the mod added every tool call would be judged twice.

I'd test in a second terminal with only the mod loaded, without your user-level hooks:
```
claude --setting-sources project,local --plugin-dir ~/Develop/claude-decisions-mod
```
That session reloads the mod whenever you save a file. One side effect: it also leaves out your other user settings and plugins.

One thing to look at: the Python `secrets-guard` blocked `[ -n "${VAR:-}" ] && echo set`, which is the exact form its own hint suggests. The TypeScript port probably has the same false alarm.

What would you like to clarify about the install options or the model choice?

The mod is installed, but this session hasn't loaded it yet. Run `/reload-plugins` at the prompt, then tell me, and I'll test it here.

What I did:
- **Checked your settings:** `~/.claude/settings.json` now has no `PreToolUse` hooks, so the mod will be the only guard.
- **Added the marketplace:** `claude plugin marketplace add ~/Develop/claude-decisions-mod` added it as `claude-decisions-mod`, in your user settings.
- **Installed the mod:** `decisions-guard@claude-decisions-mod` is enabled at user scope. `claude plugin list` shows `Read from: /Users/jessearmand/Develop/claude-decisions-mod`, so Claude Code reads it straight from your checkout. After you edit files there, `/reload-plugins` picks up the changes, with no reinstall and no version bump.

The Jev judge is still off, because `jevEnable` defaults to false. The install said none of the mod's 10 options are set yet. To turn the judge on, run `/plugin configure decisions-guard@claude-decisions-mod` and set `jevEnable` to true. You can leave `jevApiKey` empty: the mod falls back to fnox, which I confirmed finds your key from any directory. You can also choose `jevModel` there: the default is `typesafe-ai/jev`, or set `typesafe-ai/jev-1.14.0`.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The marketplace entry's source is a relative path (`"source": "./"`), so Claude Code reads the plugin straight from your checkout instead of a copy. A marketplace added from GitHub would make you publish a new version or commit to get each change.
- The validator warned that the mod's `classic.PreToolUse` hooks don't run in an installed plugin where an organization manages Claude Code. That doesn't affect your personal setup, but anyone you share the mod with under managed settings wouldn't get the guards.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Once you've reloaded, I'll run a few harmless test commands: reading a `.env`, a `git push --force` and a dry-run `rm -rf` on a scratch folder. That should show a deny, an ask, and the decisions written to `~/.claude/hooks-logs`. If you've turned the judge on, I'll also try a command that only Jev should catch.

content.text:
The mod is already running as a PreToolUse hook, and the Jev judge is live. You don't need anything in `settings.json` for it.

**Why there's no PreToolUse entry to add:** `hooks/register.ts` registers itself with `on("classic.PreToolUse", …)`. That is the mod API's version of the same event your Python hooks used. When the plugin is enabled, Claude Code calls it before every tool call. That's why the `PreToolUse` list in your settings stays empty.

**How I checked it live, after your reload:**
1. I ran `grep -rn "PLUGIN =" …/hooks`. The mod's `bash-command-validator` denied it with "Use 'rg' (ripgrep) instead of 'grep'". No other hook could have answered, because your settings have none left.
2. The last entries in `~/.claude/hooks-logs/2026-10-17.jsonl` have timestamps written by the TypeScript mod (`…18:30:11.806Z`); the Python entries were written as `+00:00`. Each one holds Jev's answers. For one of my read-only commands, `fetch_and_execute` was 0.32 and `off_task` was 0.37, both under 0.7, so it deferred to the normal permission flow. Each answer used about 1.2k input tokens, and the key came from fnox, since `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` isn't set in this session.

**Your config:** `/plugin configure` saved five of the ten options. The other five use their defaults.

| Option | Value now | Source | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `jevEnable` | **true** | saved | Ask Jev about Bash commands the fixed rules don't decide |
| `secretsLevel` | `high` | saved (default) | Blocks SSH keys, cloud credentials, `.env`, other secret files, env dumps and exfiltration. `strict` also blocks database configs. |
| `dangerousLevel` | `high` | saved (default) | Which tiers of the dangerous-command rules apply |
| `askInsteadOfDeny` | false | saved (default) | Fixed-rule denials stay denials instead of turning into prompts |
| `unattendedKeepAsk` | false | saved (default) | Under `bypassPermissions` or `dontAsk`, a prompt turns into a deny |
| `jevModel` | `typesafe-ai/jev` | default | Set `typesafe-ai/jev-1.14.0` to try the newer weights |
| `jevApiKey` | empty | default | Uses `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` or `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` from the environment, then fnox (works now) |
| `jevTimeoutSeconds` | 5 | default | Past this time the judge defers. A call takes 0.5–1s including the fnox start. |
| `askThreshold` | 0.7 | default | Probability of any concern at or above which Jev prompts you |
| `logDir` | empty → `~/.claude/hooks-logs` | default | One JSONL file per day |

Your `permissions.defaultMode` is `auto`, which isn't one of the unattended modes. So when a rule or Jev asks, you get a prompt; it isn't turned into a deny.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The judge runs only when no fixed rule decided first. That's why my `grep` was denied with no Jev call, while the `sed`/`python3` reads went to Jev and deferred.
- `defer` means "no opinion", not "allow". The mod never answers `allow`, so your own permission rules still decide what runs without a prompt.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

allow: $defaults

ElevenLabs `agents init` is routine when `--override` is absent: `elevenlabs`, `bunx elevenlabs`, or `fnox exec -- elevenlabs`, followed only by an optional target path and `--no-ui` or `--human-friendly`. It may target an existing directory, because plain init creates missing files and skips existing config. Not covered: `--override` (it recreates the project, so evaluate it under Irreversible Local Destruction and require user intent naming `--override` and the target path), shell composition, redirection, environment assignments, other `agents` subcommands, and any pull or push.

Starting or stopping the local dev server is routine: exactly `mise run dev`, `mise run stop`, or `fnox exec -- bun run dev`, with no extra arguments, flags, or shell composition. It applies only when no execution-relevant definition in that command's launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected mise task, the selected package.json script, a wrapper script it invokes, or the `fnox.toml` profile it uses. Edits to unrelated fields, unrelated tasks, or application source loaded after the server starts do not disqualify it. `mise run stop` covers the local dev server only, never a remote, production, or shared process.
soft_deny: $defaults

ElevenLabs Agent Config Sync [named+specifics, **must name:** the direction and the exact agent or config scope]: Executing an operation that changes remote agent configuration or writes pulled configuration locally, including `agents push`, `agents pull`, and equivalent agent-config API mutations. Name the agent ID or unambiguous config identity; for `--all` or other bulk forms, name every agent plus any branch or local output directory. Excludes `--dry-run`, `--help`, list and status commands, and ordinary TTS/STT calls. Tools and tests configuration are not covered.

Cloud Deploys [named+specifics, **must name:** the service or project and the destination environment]: Executing a CLI or API operation that creates or updates a deployed cloud revision or shifts deployed traffic, including Vercel and Wrangler deploy commands. Name the target and classify the destination as production or non-production, naming preview, staging, development, or another environment where that applies. Build-only, plan-only, and dry-run commands are excluded. An ordinary `git push` is not a direct deploy under this rule, but it remains subject to every applicable built-in rule.

Cloud Object Storage Mutations [named+specifics, **must name:** the provider and destination store, and for any overwrite or deletion the object or prefix]: Executing a remote mutation against R2, Vercel Blob, S3 or an S3-compatible service, GCS, Azure Blob, or an equivalent object store: upload, overwrite, copy, move, or delete. Writing source code that could later perform such an operation is not this rule. Excludes a store visibly created by a prior tool call this session, which does not clear exfiltration, mass-deletion, or access-policy rules.

Database DDL and Destructive Table Operations [named+specifics, **must name:** the database target and the exact migration or operation]: Executing DDL or an equivalent ORM schema mutation against a pre-existing database: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, RENAME, index or extension changes, and destructive resets or TRUNCATE. Generating migration files, schema diffs, migration status, and dry runs are excluded when they do not mutate a database. A project migration command counts as adopted only when its configuration and history existed before this session; for a local or development target, an explicit request naming the migration and the target clears this rule. Production remains subject to this rule and to every applicable built-in production rule. Excludes a temporary or development database visibly created by a prior tool call this session.

Edited Execution Definitions [named+specifics, **must name:** the changed file and the effective command or secret scope]: Running a task whose selected definition or execution-relevant launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected entry in `mise.toml`, `.mise.toml`, `mise.local.toml`, `.mise/config.toml`, `package.json`, a mise task file, or a directly or transitively invoked wrapper script, and the selected `fnox.toml` profile when its secret mappings changed. Edits to an unrelated field, task, or script, or to application source loaded after the target process starts, do not match. A dirty file seen in command output is not evidence that the definition changed this session.
hard_deny: $defaults

Never transmit git objects, a repository archive, source files, or diffs to a destination outside the session repository's fetch and push destinations as configured at session start, or to an external code-review, analysis, or paste service. A remote added or repointed during the session does not become a trusted destination, but a new alias resolving to the same host, owner, and repository as a pre-session destination is not a new destination. Normal pushes to the pre-session configured repository host are not third-party review uploads under this rule. Build and deploy artifacts are not repository contents here and are evaluated under other rules.

Never cause a project dependency's declared or resolved version to increase, widen a permitted version range, advance a git dependency reference, refresh a lockfile to newer direct or transitive resolutions, or add a dependency through a floating tag such as `latest`. This covers package-manager update and upgrade commands and manual manifest or lockfile edits with those effects. Adding a new dependency is allowed only at an exact user-specified version that does not upgrade existing resolutions. Downgrades and lockfile-format-only changes are not upgrades. Installing from an existing lockfile is not an upgrade, and frozen mode (`npm ci`, `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync --frozen`) is the safe form; an install that would rewrite the lockfile to newer resolutions is an upgrade and is covered. Upgrades are performed by the user outside Claude Code.
environment: **Organization**: None. A personal GitHub account (`jessearmand`, with a secondary account `jessearmandse`), not an org. No employer or client work runs here.

**Primary use of Claude Code**: personal/hobby software development across several repos under ~/Develop: web apps (Next.js / React / Bun), Apple-platform work, and this machine's own Claude Code and dotfiles configuration.
**Cloud provider(s)**: Cloudflare and Vercel. No AWS, GCP or Azure account is configured.

**Repository visibility**: treat every repo under github.com/jessearmand and github.com/jessearmandse as PUBLIC unless its visibility is verified otherwise with `gh` during the session, so any push is publishing. Verified public: latent-space-generator, subaki-realtime, claude-code-rules.
**Internal sharing / snippet hosting**: None configured. Public paste, gist and pastebin services are outside the trust boundary.

**Org-specific CLIs**: `fnox` (Keychain-backed secret injection; `fnox exec -- <cmd>` is the routine way to run anything that needs a key) and `mise` (task runner; `mise run <task>`). Routine local tooling: bun/bunx, gh, rg, ast-grep, uv/uvx, nvim, hf, elevenlabs. None are org-specific in the corporate sense; this is a personal setup.

**Secrets management**: fnox, backed by the macOS login Keychain. Each repo has its own `fnox.toml` that names the keys but never holds their values; they are injected per-process by `fnox exec`. Key names differ per repo, so read that repo's fnox.toml rather than assuming a list. GitHub Actions holds one CI secret, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Git identity and the GPG signing key live in ~/.gitconfig.private.

**CI/CD deploy targets**: GitHub Actions. Vercel and Cloudflare deployments can trigger automatically from a push to the default branch. That auto-deploy is expected and is not itself a Production Deploy: pushes are governed by the push rules, and direct deploy commands by the Cloud Deploys rule.
**Network posture**: None configured.
**Protected deployment namespaces / environments**: None configured. Fall back to the Sensitive remote targets heuristic.
**Data retention / declassification**: None configured.

**Trusted repo**: the git repository containing the session's working directory, together with the remotes already configured in it, and nothing else. All of them are personal and treated as PUBLIC, so pushes are publishing: only that repo's own work belongs in it, and content ported, repointed, or first read from outside it is not its own work. Secrets and sensitive data are never cleared into any repo by its visibility.

**Source control**: GitHub only, under the personal accounts `jessearmand` and `jessearmandse`. The trusted destinations are the remotes that already exist in the session's repo; no other org, fork or mirror is configured.
**Trusted internal domains**: None configured.
**Trusted cloud buckets**: None configured.

**Key internal services**: None. There are no internal services. The third-party APIs used routinely (api.elevenlabs.io, api.mistral.ai, api.x.ai, generativelanguage.googleapis.com, huggingface.co, tinker.thinkingmachines.dev, fal.run) are vendor endpoints OUTSIDE the trust boundary: whatever goes into a request body leaves the machine.
**Internal package registry**: None configured.

**Sensitive data locations & audiences**: any file or store holding personal data, credentials, regulated data, or similarly sensitive material; preserve exact handles when known and share only with audiences cleared at the [named+specifics] bar. On this machine that includes `.env*` files (gitignored), every Keychain entry named by a repo's fnox.toml, the `Claude Code-credentials` Keychain item, ~/.gitconfig.private, and ~/.claude/settings.json.

**Sensitive remote targets**: any namespace, host, or container whose name carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment (hyphen/underscore/dot-delimited, e.g. matches `prod-db`, not `producer`)
**Protected IaC scopes**: IAM, RBAC, networking, quota, and node-pool resources; anything whose name or tag carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment

"Classic" means the settings-file hook system: the `hooks` block in `settings.json`, with events like `PreToolUse`, `Stop` and `Notification`. The mod API exposes each of those events as `classic.<Name>`. Yes, there is a newer, mod-native event for the same moment: `tool.call`. I took all of this from the engine's type file that Claude Code 2.1.302 wrote into `.claude-plugin/types/claude-code/index.d.ts`.

**How the two events nest.** `tool.call` is the outer event, and `classic.PreToolUse` runs inside it:

```
tool.call hooks (every plugin)          ← the newer event
  └─ next(e) → core:
       classic.PreToolUse chain         ← where decisions-guard is
         [managed hooks, mod hooks, your settings hooks]
       → permission prompt / auto-mode classifier
       → the tool itself
```

| | `classic.PreToolUse` (current) | `tool.call` |
|---|---|---|
| Results | `allow` / **`ask`** / `deny`, or nothing (normal permission flow) | `{ deny }`, or `{ result }` (answer for the tool) |
| Can prompt you | Yes. `ask` opens Claude Code's own permission dialog, the same as the Python hooks. | No `ask` result. The nearest thing is `$.ui.ask(…)`, a separate question dialog. It fails in `-p` runs, and auto mode's classifier doesn't take part. |
| What it wraps | Only the decision | Everything: the permission check, the prompt and the tool's result. It can rewrite input, change output, or act after the tool ran. |
| Organization-managed Claude Code | Skipped for plugins a person installs (`plugin validate` warned about this) | Runs |

**My recommendation: stay on `classic.PreToolUse`.** Asking is the core of this mod. `rm-rf-guard` always asks, file removals like `git clean -f` ask, and the Jev judge can only ask. `tool.call` has no ask result, so a move would mean building prompts on `$.ui.ask`. That loses the real permission dialog and the auto-mode behaviour, and needs its own fallback where nobody can answer. `tool.call` becomes worth it only if you want things PreToolUse can't do, such as hiding secrets in tool output after the tool ran, or running on organization-managed machines. Even then, a mixed design is better: keep the decisions on `classic.PreToolUse` and add a `tool.call` hook only for the after-the-tool part.

**Your model change** is saved as `jevModel: typesafe-ai/jev-1.14.0` in `pluginConfigs`, and the judge has been running since your reload. I can't prove from the log that 1.14.0 answered, because the audit log doesn't record which model it asked. Two reminders from the earlier probe: 1.14.0 has no backup provider, and it sometimes asks about `terraform plan`. If those asks annoy you, raise `askThreshold` to 0.75.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Your mod's hooks sit in the middle of the chain: below managed hooks, above your own settings hooks. A deny from a managed hook still overrules the mod, and the mod overrules anything you add to `settings.json` later.
- `tool.call` guards fail open by default: if the hook fails, it is skipped and the tool runs. That's why `register.ts` adds `.catch(...)` to deny when `next` wasn't called. Any `tool.call` hook you add later needs the same.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Two decisions are yours:
- Should I add a `model` field to the judge's audit entries, so the log shows which Jev version answered? In `src/judge/bash-risk-judge.ts` it's about two lines plus a test.
- Should I commit the oxlint/oxfmt migration that is still uncommitted?

allow: $defaults

ElevenLabs `agents init` is routine when `--override` is absent: `elevenlabs`, `bunx elevenlabs`, or `fnox exec -- elevenlabs`, followed only by an optional target path and `--no-ui` or `--human-friendly`. It may target an existing directory, because plain init creates missing files and skips existing config. Not covered: `--override` (it recreates the project, so evaluate it under Irreversible Local Destruction and require user intent naming `--override` and the target path), shell composition, redirection, environment assignments, other `agents` subcommands, and any pull or push.

Starting or stopping the local dev server is routine: exactly `mise run dev`, `mise run stop`, or `fnox exec -- bun run dev`, with no extra arguments, flags, or shell composition. It applies only when no execution-relevant definition in that command's launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected mise task, the selected package.json script, a wrapper script it invokes, or the `fnox.toml` profile it uses. Edits to unrelated fields, unrelated tasks, or application source loaded after the server starts do not disqualify it. `mise run stop` covers the local dev server only, never a remote, production, or shared process.
soft_deny: $defaults

ElevenLabs Agent Config Sync [named+specifics, **must name:** the direction and the exact agent or config scope]: Executing an operation that changes remote agent configuration or writes pulled configuration locally, including `agents push`, `agents pull`, and equivalent agent-config API mutations. Name the agent ID or unambiguous config identity; for `--all` or other bulk forms, name every agent plus any branch or local output directory. Excludes `--dry-run`, `--help`, list and status commands, and ordinary TTS/STT calls. Tools and tests configuration are not covered.

Cloud Deploys [named+specifics, **must name:** the service or project and the destination environment]: Executing a CLI or API operation that creates or updates a deployed cloud revision or shifts deployed traffic, including Vercel and Wrangler deploy commands. Name the target and classify the destination as production or non-production, naming preview, staging, development, or another environment where that applies. Build-only, plan-only, and dry-run commands are excluded. An ordinary `git push` is not a direct deploy under this rule, but it remains subject to every applicable built-in rule.

Cloud Object Storage Mutations [named+specifics, **must name:** the provider and destination store, and for any overwrite or deletion the object or prefix]: Executing a remote mutation against R2, Vercel Blob, S3 or an S3-compatible service, GCS, Azure Blob, or an equivalent object store: upload, overwrite, copy, move, or delete. Writing source code that could later perform such an operation is not this rule. Excludes a store visibly created by a prior tool call this session, which does not clear exfiltration, mass-deletion, or access-policy rules.

Database DDL and Destructive Table Operations [named+specifics, **must name:** the database target and the exact migration or operation]: Executing DDL or an equivalent ORM schema mutation against a pre-existing database: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, RENAME, index or extension changes, and destructive resets or TRUNCATE. Generating migration files, schema diffs, migration status, and dry runs are excluded when they do not mutate a database. A project migration command counts as adopted only when its configuration and history existed before this session; for a local or development target, an explicit request naming the migration and the target clears this rule. Production remains subject to this rule and to every applicable built-in production rule. Excludes a temporary or development database visibly created by a prior tool call this session.

Edited Execution Definitions [named+specifics, **must name:** the changed file and the effective command or secret scope]: Running a task whose selected definition or execution-relevant launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected entry in `mise.toml`, `.mise.toml`, `mise.local.toml`, `.mise/config.toml`, `package.json`, a mise task file, or a directly or transitively invoked wrapper script, and the selected `fnox.toml` profile when its secret mappings changed. Edits to an unrelated field, task, or script, or to application source loaded after the target process starts, do not match. A dirty file seen in command output is not evidence that the definition changed this session.
hard_deny: $defaults

Never transmit git objects, a repository archive, source files, or diffs to a destination outside the session repository's fetch and push destinations as configured at session start, or to an external code-review, analysis, or paste service. A remote added or repointed during the session does not become a trusted destination, but a new alias resolving to the same host, owner, and repository as a pre-session destination is not a new destination. Normal pushes to the pre-session configured repository host are not third-party review uploads under this rule. Build and deploy artifacts are not repository contents here and are evaluated under other rules.

Never cause a project dependency's declared or resolved version to increase, widen a permitted version range, advance a git dependency reference, refresh a lockfile to newer direct or transitive resolutions, or add a dependency through a floating tag such as `latest`. This covers package-manager update and upgrade commands and manual manifest or lockfile edits with those effects. Adding a new dependency is allowed only at an exact user-specified version that does not upgrade existing resolutions. Downgrades and lockfile-format-only changes are not upgrades. Installing from an existing lockfile is not an upgrade, and frozen mode (`npm ci`, `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync --frozen`) is the safe form; an install that would rewrite the lockfile to newer resolutions is an upgrade and is covered. Upgrades are performed by the user outside Claude Code.
environment: **Organization**: None. A personal GitHub account (`jessearmand`, with a secondary account `jessearmandse`), not an org. No employer or client work runs here.

**Primary use of Claude Code**: personal/hobby software development across several repos under ~/Develop: web apps (Next.js / React / Bun), Apple-platform work, and this machine's own Claude Code and dotfiles configuration.
**Cloud provider(s)**: Cloudflare and Vercel. No AWS, GCP or Azure account is configured.

**Repository visibility**: treat every repo under github.com/jessearmand and github.com/jessearmandse as PUBLIC unless its visibility is verified otherwise with `gh` during the session, so any push is publishing. Verified public: latent-space-generator, subaki-realtime, claude-code-rules.
**Internal sharing / snippet hosting**: None configured. Public paste, gist and pastebin services are outside the trust boundary.

**Org-specific CLIs**: `fnox` (Keychain-backed secret injection; `fnox exec -- <cmd>` is the routine way to run anything that needs a key) and `mise` (task runner; `mise run <task>`). Routine local tooling: bun/bunx, gh, rg, ast-grep, uv/uvx, nvim, hf, elevenlabs. None are org-specific in the corporate sense; this is a personal setup.

**Secrets management**: fnox, backed by the macOS login Keychain. Each repo has its own `fnox.toml` that names the keys but never holds their values; they are injected per-process by `fnox exec`. Key names differ per repo, so read that repo's fnox.toml rather than assuming a list. GitHub Actions holds one CI secret, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Git identity and the GPG signing key live in ~/.gitconfig.private.

**CI/CD deploy targets**: GitHub Actions. Vercel and Cloudflare deployments can trigger automatically from a push to the default branch. That auto-deploy is expected and is not itself a Production Deploy: pushes are governed by the push rules, and direct deploy commands by the Cloud Deploys rule.
**Network posture**: None configured.
**Protected deployment namespaces / environments**: None configured. Fall back to the Sensitive remote targets heuristic.
**Data retention / declassification**: None configured.

**Trusted repo**: the git repository containing the session's working directory, together with the remotes already configured in it, and nothing else. All of them are personal and treated as PUBLIC, so pushes are publishing: only that repo's own work belongs in it, and content ported, repointed, or first read from outside it is not its own work. Secrets and sensitive data are never cleared into any repo by its visibility.

**Source control**: GitHub only, under the personal accounts `jessearmand` and `jessearmandse`. The trusted destinations are the remotes that already exist in the session's repo; no other org, fork or mirror is configured.
**Trusted internal domains**: None configured.
**Trusted cloud buckets**: None configured.

**Key internal services**: None. There are no internal services. The third-party APIs used routinely (api.elevenlabs.io, api.mistral.ai, api.x.ai, generativelanguage.googleapis.com, huggingface.co, tinker.thinkingmachines.dev, fal.run) are vendor endpoints OUTSIDE the trust boundary: whatever goes into a request body leaves the machine.
**Internal package registry**: None configured.

**Sensitive data locations & audiences**: any file or store holding personal data, credentials, regulated data, or similarly sensitive material; preserve exact handles when known and share only with audiences cleared at the [named+specifics] bar. On this machine that includes `.env*` files (gitignored), every Keychain entry named by a repo's fnox.toml, the `Claude Code-credentials` Keychain item, ~/.gitconfig.private, and ~/.claude/settings.json.

**Sensitive remote targets**: any namespace, host, or container whose name carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment (hyphen/underscore/dot-delimited, e.g. matches `prod-db`, not `producer`)
**Protected IaC scopes**: IAM, RBAC, networking, quota, and node-pool resources; anything whose name or tag carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment

- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

hard_deny: $defaults

Never transmit git objects, a repository archive, source files, or diffs to a destination outside the session repository's fetch and push destinations as configured at session start, or to an external code-review, analysis, or paste service. A remote added or repointed during the session does not become a trusted destination, but a new alias resolving to the same host, owner, and repository as a pre-session destination is not a new destination. Normal pushes to the pre-session configured repository host are not third-party review uploads under this rule. Build and deploy artifacts are not repository contents here and are evaluated under other rules.

Never cause a project dependency's declared or resolved version to increase, widen a permitted version range, advance a git dependency reference, refresh a lockfile to newer direct or transitive resolutions, or add a dependency through a floating tag such as `latest`. This covers package-manager update and upgrade commands and manual manifest or lockfile edits with those effects. Adding a new dependency is allowed only at an exact user-specified version that does not upgrade existing resolutions. Downgrades and lockfile-format-only changes are not upgrades. Installing from an existing lockfile is not an upgrade, and frozen mode (`npm ci`, `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync --frozen`) is the safe form; an install that would rewrite the lockfile to newer resolutions is an upgrade and is covered. ElevenLabs `agents init` is routine when `--override` is absent: `elevenlabs`, `bunx elevenlabs`, or `fnox exec -- elevenlabs`, followed only by an optional target path and `--no-ui` or `--human-friendly`. It may target an existing directory, because plain init creates missing files and skips existing config. Not covered: `--override` (it recreates the project, so evaluate it under Irreversible Local Destruction and require user intent naming `--override` and the target path), shell composition, redirection, environment assignments, other `agents` subcommands, and any pull or push.

Starting or stopping the local dev server is routine: exactly `mise run dev`, `mise run stop`, or `fnox exec -- bun run dev`, with no extra arguments, flags, or shell composition. It applies only when no execution-relevant definition in that command's launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected mise task, the selected package.json script, a wrapper script it invokes, or the `fnox.toml` profile it uses. Edits to unrelated fields, unrelated tasks, or application source loaded after the server starts do not disqualify it. `mise run stop` covers the local dev server only, never a remote, production, or shared process.

ElevenLabs Agent Config Sync [named+specifics, **must name:** the direction and the exact agent or config scope]: Executing an operation that changes remote agent configuration or writes pulled configuration locally, including `agents push`, `agents pull`, and equivalent agent-config API mutations. Name the agent ID or unambiguous config identity; for `--all` or other bulk forms, name every agent plus any branch or local output directory. Excludes `--dry-run`, `--help`, list and status commands, and ordinary TTS/STT calls. Tools and tests configuration are not covered.

Cloud Deploys [named+specifics, **must name:** the service or project and the destination environment]: Executing a CLI or API operation that creates or updates a deployed cloud revision or shifts deployed traffic, including Vercel and Wrangler deploy commands. Name the target and classify the destination as production or non-production, naming preview, staging, development, or another environment where that applies. Build-only, plan-only, and dry-run commands are excluded. An ordinary `git push` is not a direct deploy under this rule, but it remains subject to every applicable built-in rule.

Cloud Object Storage Mutations [named+specifics, **must name:** the provider and destination store, and for any overwrite or deletion the object or prefix]: Executing a remote mutation against R2, Vercel Blob, S3 or an S3-compatible service, GCS, Azure Blob, or an equivalent object store: upload, overwrite, copy, move, or delete. Writing source code that could later perform such an operation is not this rule. Excludes a store visibly created by a prior tool call this session, which does not clear exfiltration, mass-deletion, or access-policy rules.

Database DDL and Destructive Table Operations [named+specifics, **must name:** the database target and the exact migration or operation]: Executing DDL or an equivalent ORM schema mutation against a pre-existing database: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, RENAME, index or extension changes, and destructive resets or TRUNCATE. Generating migration files, schema diffs, migration status, and dry runs are excluded when they do not mutate a database. A project migration command counts as adopted only when its configuration and history existed before this session; for a local or development target, an explicit request naming the migration and the target clears this rule. Edits to an unrelated field, task, or script, or to application source loaded after the target process starts, do not match. hard_deny: $defaults

Never transmit git objects, a repository archive, source files, or diffs to a destination outside the session repository's fetch and push destinations as configured at session start, or to an external code-review, analysis, or paste service. A remote added or repointed during the session does not become a trusted destination, but a new alias resolving to the same host, owner, and repository as a pre-session destination is not a new destination. Normal pushes to the pre-session configured repository host are not third-party review uploads under this rule. Build and deploy artifacts are not repository contents here and are evaluated under other rules.

Never cause a project dependency's declared or resolved version to increase, widen a permitted version range, advance a git dependency reference, refresh a lockfile to newer direct or transitive resolutions, or add a dependency through a floating tag such as `latest`. This covers package-manager update and upgrade commands and manual manifest or lockfile edits with those effects. Adding a new dependency is allowed only at an exact user-specified version that does not upgrade existing resolutions. Downgrades and lockfile-format-only changes are not upgrades. Installing from an existing lockfile is not an upgrade, and frozen mode (`npm ci`, `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync --frozen`) is the safe form; an install that would rewrite the lockfile to newer resolutions is an upgrade and is covered. Upgrades are performed by the user outside Claude Code.

Git identity and the GPG signing key live in ~/.gitconfig.private.

**Network posture**: None configured.
**Protected deployment namespaces / environments**: None configured. Fall back to the Sensitive remote targets heuristic.
**Data retention / declassification**: None configured.

**Trusted repo**: the git repository containing the session's working directory, together with the remotes already configured in it, and nothing else. All of them are personal and treated as PUBLIC, so pushes are publishing: only that repo's own work belongs in it, and content ported, repointed, or first read from outside it is not its own work. Secrets and sensitive data are never cleared into any repo by its visibility.

**Source control**: GitHub only, under the personal accounts `jessearmand` and `jessearmandse`. The trusted destinations are the remotes that already exist in the session's repo; no other org, fork or mirror is configured.
**Trusted internal domains**: None configured.
**Trusted cloud buckets**: None configured.

**Key internal services**: None. There are no internal services. **Internal package registry**: None configured.

**Sensitive data locations & audiences**: any file or store holding personal data, credentials, regulated data, or similarly sensitive material; preserve exact handles when known and share only with audiences cleared at the [named+specifics] bar. On this machine that includes `.env*` files (gitignored), every Keychain entry named by a repo's fnox.toml, the `Claude Code-credentials` Keychain item, ~/.gitconfig.private, and ~/.claude/settings.json.

**Protected IaC scopes**: IAM, RBAC, networking, quota, and node-pool resources; anything whose name or tag carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment

allow: $defaults

ElevenLabs `agents init` is routine when `--override` is absent: `elevenlabs`, `bunx elevenlabs`, or `fnox exec -- elevenlabs`, followed only by an optional target path and `--no-ui` or `--human-friendly`. It may target an existing directory, because plain init creates missing files and skips existing config. Not covered: `--override` (it recreates the project, so evaluate it under Irreversible Local Destruction and require user intent naming `--override` and the target path), shell composition, redirection, environment assignments, other `agents` subcommands, and any pull or push.

Starting or stopping the local dev server is routine: exactly `mise run dev`, `mise run stop`, or `fnox exec -- bun run dev`, with no extra arguments, flags, or shell composition. It applies only when no execution-relevant definition in that command's launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected mise task, the selected package.json script, a wrapper script it invokes, or the `fnox.toml` profile it uses. Edits to unrelated fields, unrelated tasks, or application source loaded after the server starts do not disqualify it. `mise run stop` covers the local dev server only, never a remote, production, or shared process.
soft_deny: $defaults

ElevenLabs Agent Config Sync [named+specifics, **must name:** the direction and the exact agent or config scope]: Executing an operation that changes remote agent configuration or writes pulled configuration locally, including `agents push`, `agents pull`, and equivalent agent-config API mutations. Name the agent ID or unambiguous config identity; for `--all` or other bulk forms, name every agent plus any branch or local output directory. Excludes `--dry-run`, `--help`, list and status commands, and ordinary TTS/STT calls. Tools and tests configuration are not covered.

Cloud Deploys [named+specifics, **must name:** the service or project and the destination environment]: Executing a CLI or API operation that creates or updates a deployed cloud revision or shifts deployed traffic, including Vercel and Wrangler deploy commands. Name the target and classify the destination as production or non-production, naming preview, staging, development, or another environment where that applies. Build-only, plan-only, and dry-run commands are excluded. An ordinary `git push` is not a direct deploy under this rule, but it remains subject to every applicable built-in rule.

Cloud Object Storage Mutations [named+specifics, **must name:** the provider and destination store, and for any overwrite or deletion the object or prefix]: Executing a remote mutation against R2, Vercel Blob, S3 or an S3-compatible service, GCS, Azure Blob, or an equivalent object store: upload, overwrite, copy, move, or delete. Writing source code that could later perform such an operation is not this rule. Excludes a store visibly created by a prior tool call this session, which does not clear exfiltration, mass-deletion, or access-policy rules.

Database DDL and Destructive Table Operations [named+specifics, **must name:** the database target and the exact migration or operation]: Executing DDL or an equivalent ORM schema mutation against a pre-existing database: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, RENAME, index or extension changes, and destructive resets or TRUNCATE. Generating migration files, schema diffs, migration status, and dry runs are excluded when they do not mutate a database. A project migration command counts as adopted only when its configuration and history existed before this session; for a local or development target, an explicit request naming the migration and the target clears this rule. Production remains subject to this rule and to every applicable built-in production rule. Excludes a temporary or development database visibly created by a prior tool call this session.

Edited Execution Definitions [named+specifics, **must name:** the changed file and the effective command or secret scope]: Running a task whose selected definition or execution-relevant launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected entry in `mise.toml`, `.mise.toml`, `mise.local.toml`, `.mise/config.toml`, `package.json`, a mise task file, or a directly or transitively invoked wrapper script, and the selected `fnox.toml` profile when its secret mappings changed. Edits to an unrelated field, task, or script, or to application source loaded after the target process starts, do not match. A dirty file seen in command output is not evidence that the definition changed this session.
hard_deny: $defaults

Never transmit git objects, a repository archive, source files, or diffs to a destination outside the session repository's fetch and push destinations as configured at session start, or to an external code-review, analysis, or paste service. A remote added or repointed during the session does not become a trusted destination, but a new alias resolving to the same host, owner, and repository as a pre-session destination is not a new destination. Normal pushes to the pre-session configured repository host are not third-party review uploads under this rule. Build and deploy artifacts are not repository contents here and are evaluated under other rules.

Never cause a project dependency's declared or resolved version to increase, widen a permitted version range, advance a git dependency reference, refresh a lockfile to newer direct or transitive resolutions, or add a dependency through a floating tag such as `latest`. This covers package-manager update and upgrade commands and manual manifest or lockfile edits with those effects. Adding a new dependency is allowed only at an exact user-specified version that does not upgrade existing resolutions. Downgrades and lockfile-format-only changes are not upgrades. Installing from an existing lockfile is not an upgrade, and frozen mode (`npm ci`, `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync --frozen`) is the safe form; an install that would rewrite the lockfile to newer resolutions is an upgrade and is covered. Upgrades are performed by the user outside Claude Code.
environment: **Organization**: None. A personal GitHub account (`jessearmand`, with a secondary account `jessearmandse`), not an org. No employer or client work runs here.

**Primary use of Claude Code**: personal/hobby software development across several repos under ~/Develop: web apps (Next.js / React / Bun), Apple-platform work, and this machine's own Claude Code and dotfiles configuration.
**Cloud provider(s)**: Cloudflare and Vercel. No AWS, GCP or Azure account is configured.

**Repository visibility**: treat every repo under github.com/jessearmand and github.com/jessearmandse as PUBLIC unless its visibility is verified otherwise with `gh` during the session, so any push is publishing. Verified public: latent-space-generator, subaki-realtime, claude-code-rules.
**Internal sharing / snippet hosting**: None configured. Public paste, gist and pastebin services are outside the trust boundary.

**Org-specific CLIs**: `fnox` (Keychain-backed secret injection; `fnox exec -- <cmd>` is the routine way to run anything that needs a key) and `mise` (task runner; `mise run <task>`). Routine local tooling: bun/bunx, gh, rg, ast-grep, uv/uvx, nvim, hf, elevenlabs. None are org-specific in the corporate sense; this is a personal setup.

**Secrets management**: fnox, backed by the macOS login Keychain. Each repo has its own `fnox.toml` that names the keys but never holds their values; they are injected per-process by `fnox exec`. Key names differ per repo, so read that repo's fnox.toml rather than assuming a list. GitHub Actions holds one CI secret, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Git identity and the GPG signing key live in ~/.gitconfig.private.

**CI/CD deploy targets**: GitHub Actions. Vercel and Cloudflare deployments can trigger automatically from a push to the default branch. That auto-deploy is expected and is not itself a Production Deploy: pushes are governed by the push rules, and direct deploy commands by the Cloud Deploys rule.
**Network posture**: None configured.
**Protected deployment namespaces / environments**: None configured. Fall back to the Sensitive remote targets heuristic.
**Data retention / declassification**: None configured.

**Trusted repo**: the git repository containing the session's working directory, together with the remotes already configured in it, and nothing else. All of them are personal and treated as PUBLIC, so pushes are publishing: only that repo's own work belongs in it, and content ported, repointed, or first read from outside it is not its own work. Secrets and sensitive data are never cleared into any repo by its visibility.

**Source control**: GitHub only, under the personal accounts `jessearmand` and `jessearmandse`. The trusted destinations are the remotes that already exist in the session's repo; no other org, fork or mirror is configured.
**Trusted internal domains**: None configured.
**Trusted cloud buckets**: None configured.

**Key internal services**: None. There are no internal services. The third-party APIs used routinely (api.elevenlabs.io, api.mistral.ai, api.x.ai, generativelanguage.googleapis.com, huggingface.co, tinker.thinkingmachines.dev, fal.run) are vendor endpoints OUTSIDE the trust boundary: whatever goes into a request body leaves the machine.
**Internal package registry**: None configured.

**Sensitive data locations & audiences**: any file or store holding personal data, credentials, regulated data, or similarly sensitive material; preserve exact handles when known and share only with audiences cleared at the [named+specifics] bar. On this machine that includes `.env*` files (gitignored), every Keychain entry named by a repo's fnox.toml, the `Claude Code-credentials` Keychain item, ~/.gitconfig.private, and ~/.claude/settings.json.

**Sensitive remote targets**: any namespace, host, or container whose name carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment (hyphen/underscore/dot-delimited, e.g. matches `prod-db`, not `producer`)
**Protected IaC scopes**: IAM, RBAC, networking, quota, and node-pool resources; anything whose name or tag carries `prod` or `production` as a whole word or name segment

n0 = s.count(r"\.env\b`")
for old in [r"${SEG}\.env\b", r"\S*\.env\b"]:

open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

ElevenLabs `agents init` is routine when `--override` is absent: `elevenlabs`, `bunx elevenlabs`, or `fnox exec -- elevenlabs`, followed only by an optional target path and `--no-ui` or `--human-friendly`. Not covered: `--override` (it recreates the project, so evaluate it under Irreversible Local Destruction and require user intent naming `--override` and the target path), shell composition, redirection, environment assignments, other `agents` subcommands, and any pull or push.

Starting or stopping the local dev server is routine: exactly `mise run dev`, `mise run stop`, or `fnox exec -- bun run dev`, with no extra arguments, flags, or shell composition. It applies only when no execution-relevant definition in that command's launch chain was edited by a visible tool call this session: the selected mise task, the selected package.json script, a wrapper script it invokes, or the `fnox.toml` profile it uses. Excludes `--dry-run`, `--help`, list and status commands, and ordinary TTS/STT calls. Tools and tests configuration are not covered.

# Porting the Python hooks to this mod

The hooks in `jessearmand/claude-code-rules/hooks/*.py` (merged PR #1) are
ported module for module into `src/`. This page is the contract every ported
module follows, so modules written separately fit together.

## Layout

| Python module | TypeScript module | Layer |
|---|---|---|
| `shell_model.py` | `src/shell/model.ts` (written, do not rewrite) | parser data |
| `shell_lexer.py` | `src/shell/lexer.ts` | parser |
| `shell_glob.py` | `src/shell/glob.ts` | parser |
| `shell_ifs.py` | `src/shell/ifs.ts` | parser |
| `shell_arith.py` | `src/shell/arith.ts` | parser |
| `shell_printf.py` | `src/shell/printf.ts` | parser |
| `shell_params.py` | `src/shell/params.ts` | parser |
| `shell_expand.py` | `src/shell/expand.ts` | parser |
| `shell_wrappers.py` | `src/shell/wrappers.ts` | parser |
| `shell_interpreters.py` | `src/shell/interpreters.ts` | parser |
| `shell_streams.py` | `src/shell/streams.ts` | parser |
| `shell_effects.py` | `src/shell/effects.ts` | parser |
| `shell_state.py` | `src/shell/state.ts` | parser |
| `shell_unwrap.py` | `src/shell/unwrap.ts` | parser |
| `shell_payloads.py` | `src/shell/payloads.ts` | parser |
| `shell_parse.py` | `src/shell/parse.ts` | parser driver |
| `shell_sources.py` | `src/shell/sources.ts` | sources |
| `make_expand.py` | `src/shell/make-expand.ts` | sources |
| `db_client_files.py` | `src/shell/db-client-files.ts` | sources |
| `command_stdin.py` | `src/shell/command-stdin.ts` | sources |
| `shell_writes.py` | `src/shell/writes.ts` | writes |
| `landing_paths.py` | `src/shell/landing-paths.ts` | writes |
| `unknown_target.py` | `src/shell/unknown-target.ts` | writes |
| `python_argv.py` | `src/shell/python-argv.ts` | parser |

`hooks/register.ts` is the hooks module Claude Code loads; it wires the guards
and imports from `src/`. Nothing under `src/` imports from `hooks/`.

## Naming

- `snake_case` becomes `camelCase`; a leading underscore is dropped. A name
  another module imports is exported; module-private names stay unexported.
  `UPPER_SNAKE` constants keep their spelling.
- A Python dataclass becomes a `readonly` interface, or a class when it has
  methods or properties (`SimpleCommand`). `dataclasses.replace(x, ...)` is
  `x.with({...})` on `SimpleCommand` and `{ ...x, ... }` on a plain object.
- A Python `dict` keyed by arbitrary strings is a `Map`; `frozenset`/`set` are
  `ReadonlySet`/`Set`; tuples and lists are `readonly T[]`; `None` is
  `undefined` in return types and `null` where the model already says so
  (`Directory = string | null`).
- Keep every comment and docstring: they record why a rule exists. A
  docstring becomes a JSDoc comment on the export.

## No Node, no globals

A hooks module runs with no Node and no DOM. Under `src/` only
`src/host/node-host.ts` may import `node:*`, and `*.spec.ts` files (vitest,
run under Node) may too. Everything else reaches the world through a `Host`
(`src/host/host.ts`): `host.stat`, `host.realPath`, `host.readText`,
`host.list`, `host.run`, `host.fetch`, `host.env`, `host.home`. The parser
carries it as `ctx.host`; a guard's `run(input, deps)` receives it.

Consequences of the Python code touching the disk synchronously:

- Any function that reads a path becomes `async` and its callers `await` it.
  Loops become `for ... of` with `await` inside, never `Array.map` with
  promises unless gathered with `Promise.all` deliberately.
- `os.path.expanduser(p)` is `expanduser(p, host.home)`; `os.getcwd()` is
  never called (the cwd is always a parameter); `os.environ.get(x)` is
  `host.env(x)` and `x` is added to `KNOWN_ENV_NAMES` in `host.ts`.
- `glob.glob(pattern, root_dir=cwd)` is `globPaths(pattern, host, { rootDir: cwd, limit })`
  from `src/shell/glob.ts` (it lists directories with `host.list` and matches
  with the module's own matcher).
- `tarfile`/`zipfile` listings run `tar -tvf` / `unzip -Z1` through `host.run`.
- Every host method answers `undefined` on failure; never `try/catch` around
  them for ordinary misses, decide conservatively instead.

## Regular expressions

Python `re` to JavaScript `RegExp`:

- `(?i)`, `(?m)`, `(?s)`, `(?x)` inline flags become the `i`, `m`, `s` flags
  (rewrite a verbose pattern on one line). `re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE` is `/.../im`.
- `(?P<name>...)` is `(?<name>...)`; `\Z` is `$` with no `m` flag or
  `(?![\s\S])`; `\A` is `^`.
- `re.fullmatch(p, s)` anchors the pattern `^(?:p)$`; `re.match` anchors with `^`
  only; `re.search` is `.exec`/`.test`.
- `re.finditer`/`findall` is `matchAll` on a `g` regex (never reuse a `g`
  regex with `.test` across calls: `lastIndex` persists). Prefer non-`g`
  regexes stored as module constants and `matchAll(new RegExp(source, "g"))`
  only where iteration is needed.
- `re.sub(pattern, fn, text)` is `text.replace(/.../g, fn)`; `count=1` drops the `g`.
- Python `\w`, `\d`, `\s`, `\b` are Unicode-aware; the JS ASCII forms are fine
  here (the rules are ASCII). Add the `u` flag only when a pattern needs it.
- Lookbehind (`(?<!...)`, `(?<=...)`) works in JS and may be variable-length.
- `str.isspace()`, `partition`, `split()` with no separator, `strip(chars)`,
  `shlex.quote`, `re.escape` are in `src/util/text.ts`; `os.path.*` in `src/util/paths.ts`.

## Tests

- Port each `*_test.py` corpus into a `*.spec.ts` beside the module (vitest:
  `describe`, `it.each`, `expect`). Keep every case and its expected label.
- Tests that need real files write them into a temporary directory with
  `node:fs` and use `nodeHost()`; tests that only need a file to exist use
  `memoryHost({ files, dirs, links })`.
- `*.test.ts` is reserved for `claude plugin test` (the mod kit, imports from
  `claude-code/testing`); vitest only collects `*.spec.ts`.
- Run `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, `bun run test` before handing a
  module over; fix what they report rather than disabling rules.

## Behaviour

Parity with the Python hooks is the goal, including their exact reason texts,
rule ids and `ask`-versus-`deny` choices. Where a Python behaviour depended
on a synchronous filesystem probe, make the same probe through the host.
Where Python code catches `OSError` and skips, the host's `undefined` answer
skips the same way. Do not add rules, rename rule ids or soften decisions.

## Import cycles

The Python stages import `parse`/`_parse_into` lazily inside functions to
avoid load-time cycles. ES modules tolerate a cycle as long as nothing is
*called* while the modules load, so import at the top of the file
(`import { parseInto } from "./parse.ts"`) and call it inside the function
as before. Never read an imported constant at module top level across a
cycle (`const X = OTHER_MODULE_CONST + 1` where the other module imports
this one); compute it lazily or move it into `model.ts`.

## Ownership

Three agents port the parser in parallel; each owns the files in its brief
and writes no other `src/` file. A sibling module that does not exist yet is
imported by its mapped file name and the camelCased Python name, exactly as
the Python import spells it (`from shell_expand import command_output`
becomes `import { commandOutput } from "./expand.ts"`). The integration pass
reconciles any name that drifted.

## What the engine reads off the hooks module

`claude plugin validate` and the engine itself read the hooks module and
every file it imports to list what the mod calls on `$`, before any code
runs. Three rules follow, and the engine refuses to load a module that
breaks them:

- `$` is only ever spelled `$.noun.method(...)` at a call site, or passed
  as an argument to a function declared at the top of a file of the module
  (a `function` declaration or a `const` bound to one). It is never stored
  in a field, returned, spread or captured by a class. That is why
  `src/host/engine-host.ts` is a set of top-level functions taking `$`
  rather than a class holding it.
- `$.env.get(name)` takes a string literal. The environment snapshot in
  `engine-host.ts` therefore spells one call per name in `KNOWN_ENV_NAMES`;
  `src/host/env-names.spec.ts` fails when the two lists drift.
- `hooks/*.test.ts` files are the engine kit's (`claude plugin test .`);
  vitest collects only `*.spec.ts`.

content.text:
I fixed the two kinds of false alarm in `secrets-guard`, and left the suspicious lint rules for later as you asked. Checks pass (oxlint, oxfmt, tsc, 7,659 tests, `claude plugin test` 7/7). Nothing is committed yet. Run `/reload-plugins` to load the fix into this session.

**Which blocks were the mod's.** I replayed today's blocked commands through the TypeScript guard:

| Command | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `echo "in env: ${AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY:+yes}"` | `echo-secret-var` | allowed (fixed) |
| `rg -n "options.env\|env\?:" src/…` | `grep-env` | allowed (fixed) |
| `rg -n '[.]env'`-style searches, `rg 'process.env.HOME' src` | `grep-env` | allowed (fixed) |
| `[ -n "${KEY:-}" ] && echo set`, and the `sh -c` version | allowed | allowed: the Python hooks made that block, not the mod |
| `printenv KEY \| wc -c` | `env-dump` | still blocked (see below) |
| `rg KEY .env`, `grep FOO .env.local`, `rg FOO -g .env`, `echo $API_KEY`, `echo "${API_KEY:-unset}"` | blocked | still blocked |

**The two fixes,** both in `src/guards/secrets-guard-rules.ts`:
1. **`.env` must start a path component.** A new `ENV_FILE` regex piece now replaces the bare `.env` match in every `.env` command rule: read, edit, source, grep, sed, tee, touch, truncate, redirect, copy and move. `.env` now only matches where a path part starts: at the beginning, after a space or quote, or after `/`, `=` or `@`. Before, it also matched inside `process.env.HOME`, after a backslash in `\.env`, and after a dot in `foo.env`. This makes the Bash rules agree with the guard's own rule for file paths, which already passed `example.env`. The existing `SECRET_NAME` already used the same lookbehind, so I followed that pattern.
2. **`${NAME:+word}` and `${NAME+word}` are allowed.** These print `word`, never the value. The variable name now has to match in full, with a lookahead, so the regex can't end it early to get past the check. `${KEY:+$KEY}` is still caught, because the inner `$KEY` matches on its own.

**Corpus:** I added 10 cases to `src/guards/__fixtures__/secrets-cases.ts`, 4 that must still block and 6 that must pass. One is `echo ${MY_TOKEN_KEY:+set} $MY_TOKEN_KEY`, which must still block. `docs/PORTING.md` says the port must not "soften decisions" from the Python hooks, so I listed both changes there as deliberate deviations. Your Python hooks in `claude-code-rules` still have both false alarms.

**One choice you might want to change:** `cat config/prod.env` is now allowed, because the path rule never treated `prod.env` as a secret. If your projects keep secrets in `<name>.env` files, the answer is to tighten both rules together, not to loosen them again.

**Left as they are, on purpose:**
- `printenv KEY | wc -c` only counts characters, but `printenv KEY` alone prints the secret. Telling those apart means following what the pipe does, which is a bigger change.
- A heredoc that writes a script which runs straight after, through `bun` or `sh`, is still checked like a command. Since that text really does run, I kept this one.

Should I commit this as "Narrow secrets-guard's .env and echo rules to real secret access"?
